name: Koesisters
summary: Spiced Cape Malay doughnuts: soft oval buns fragrant with aniseed, cinnamon, cardamom and naartjie, dipped in hot syrup and rolled in coconut.
about: Not to be confused with the plaited, crunchy Afrikaans koeksister, the Cape Malay koesister is soft, cake-like and spiced. Families in the Bo-Kaap and across the Cape Flats make them on Saturday night or early on Sunday morning, and the tradition of buying or sharing koesisters with Sunday breakfast is still strong.

ingredients.name: Sunflower oil
ingredients.note: for deep-frying, plus a little for your hands

steps: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar, all the ground spices, naartjie zest, baking powder and salt in a large bowl.
Warm the butter and milk in a small pot over low heat just until the butter melts, then add the lukewarm water; it should feel warm, not hot, on your wrist. Beat in the egg.
Pour the liquid into the dry ingredients and mix, then knead in the bowl or on a lightly floured surface for 8 to 10 minutes, until you have a soft, smooth, slightly sticky dough.
Cover the bowl with a damp cloth and leave in a warm place for about 1 hour 30 minutes, until doubled in size.
Oil your hands and divide the dough into 24 pieces, about the size of a large egg. Shape each into a smooth oval about 7 cm long, set on an oiled tray, cover and rest for 15 minutes.

Meanwhile make the syrup: bring the water, sugar, cinnamon, cardamom and naartjie peel to the boil in a wide pot, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then simmer for 10 minutes until slightly syrupy. Keep it hot on the lowest heat.

Heat the oil in a deep pot to 160 °C (a cube of bread browns in about 60 seconds). Fry 5 or 6 koesisters at a time for 2 to 3 minutes a side, until deep golden brown and cooked through. Drain on paper towel.
While they are still warm, drop the koesisters a few at a time into the hot syrup for 1 minute, turning once so they soak it up.
Lift them out with a slotted spoon, let the excess syrup drip off, then roll in the coconut. Serve warm or at room temperature the same day.
prepNote: Make the dough the night before and let it rise slowly in the fridge; shape and fry in the morning. Best eaten the day they are made.
